title: Greedy Best-First in San Francisco: Rush Mode ⚡
description: Watch Greedy Best-First grab the shortest-looking route to the goal using only the heuristic. In this San Francisco (SOMA) visualization, we’ll see exactly why it can look brilliant early—and fail catastrophically when the heuristic lies.
ig_caption:
Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison—Why it rushes to the goal ⚡

In this reel, the map is a graph and every intersection is a node. Greedy Best-First uses ONLY the heuristic h(n) (e.g., straight-line distance to the destination) and ignores the actual path cost so far.

🔥 What you’ll see:
• It expands the “closest-to-goal-looking” frontier first (fast focus).
• It may take a dead-end detour because it never “pays attention” to accumulated cost.
• It can outperform A* on easy maps, but lose badly when obstacles/one-way constraints break the heuristic.

✅ Takeaway: Greedy Best-First = speed to the goal signal, not guaranteed least-cost.

Debate question: If the heuristic is slightly wrong (city blocks + bridges), would you rather optimize for quick progress (Greedy) or guaranteed optimality (A*)?

Greedy Best-First Search vs A*: Pathfinding Comparison — Why Greedy Best-First Search rushes toward destinations and when it fails ⚡

In this San Francisco (SOMA) visualization, we run heuristic pathfinding using Greedy Best-First (priority = h(n) only) and compare the behavior you typically see versus A* (which accounts for actual cost-so-far + heuristic).

You’ll learn mechanics: graph nodes, frontier expansion order, heuristic pathfinding, and the key failure mode when the heuristic misleads.
